source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 3 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section B is the chief audit executive's decision on where internal audit spends its time. It covers where candidate engagements come from, how the organizationwide risk assessment ranks them into a plan the board approves, how the plan stays current, and how other providers' assurance is coordinated and relied on. Part 2 plans one engagement; this section plans the whole function's period.
analogy: Think of a city's road maintenance chief planning the year. The chief lists every street, rates each by traffic, wear and accident history, and adds the work that law or the mayor's office requires. The city council approves the program and any big change to it. When a flood hits, the chief reorders the work and tells the council at once. The water company and the gas utility also dig up streets, so the chief lines up schedules with them and inspects their repaving before counting it as done.

topics.overview: The audit universe is the chief audit executive's map of what could be audited. Engagements reach the plan from that map and from requests, laws, regulators, trends and change; each source is weighed by risk, never added or refused automatically.
can_do: Describe how an audit universe is built from objectives and linked to key risks
Identify the parts of an audit universe and the cross-cutting risks that span them
Describe how requests, legal mandates, trends and new technologies reach the plan
Recognize when a Topical Requirement applies to planned work, and explain why some areas recur on a cycle

subtopics.name: Building the Audit Universe
subtopics.definition: The audit universe is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) organized list of auditable units, such as business units, processes, programs and systems, linked to key risks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A risk assessment can only rank what it can see. A universe tied to objectives and key risks shows where assurance exists and where nobody is looking.
how_it_works: May (Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan): group auditable units into an audit universe; the considerations offer it as one approach, not a requirement.
Sound practice: build it from objectives and strategic initiatives, aligned with the structure or risk framework; units are business units, processes, programs or systems.
May: link each unit to its key risks.
Should: give due weight to risks that span several units, such as ethics, fraud, IT, third parties and regulatory compliance.
Should: validate key risks independently, and rely on management's risk information only after concluding its risk management processes are effective.
Must: whatever the tool, the plan rests on the CAE's documented assessment of strategies, objectives and risks, done at least annually.
subtopics.example: At a Chilean water utility, CAE Valentina rebuilds the audit universe around five strategic objectives instead of the department list. Treatment plants, billing, meter replacement and the asset system become units linked to their key risks. Contractor risk appears under three units, so Valentina records it once as a cross-cutting risk.

review: Trace each strategic objective to at least one auditable unit
Compare the audit universe with the organization chart and risk register
Inspect when the universe was last refreshed for organizational changes
evidence: Universe listing with owner, objective and risk rating per unit
Documented annual risk assessment showing its date and inputs
Board minutes where the CAE discussed the universe
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive link every auditable unit to objectives and key risks and refresh the universe when the organization changes.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive designs the universe; plan approval is in 3B2.2

subtopics.isaca_rule: An audit universe is a planning tool, not a requirement or a promise to audit everything. Must: the plan rests on the CAE's documented, at least annual risk assessment.

exam_traps.trap: Every unit in the audit universe must be audited every year.
exam_traps.why: The universe lists what could be audited; risk ranking decides what is. Lower-risk units may wait, and the CAE reports the coverage impact.

exam_traps.trap: Management's risk register can serve as internal audit's risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: Should: validate key risks independently and rely on management's information only after concluding its risk management processes are effective.

key_terms.definition: Internal audit's list of the units, processes and systems that could be audited.
A risk that spans several units or processes, such as fraud or third-party risk, and needs a joined-up evaluation.
A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.

subtopics.memory_aid: Objectives first, then units, then linked risks, then the ranking.

subtopics.name: Requests, Laws and Regulatory Mandates
subtopics.definition: Requests and mandates are engagement sources beyond the chief audit executive's (CAE's) risk ranking: asks from the board or management, and audits required by law or regulators.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Requests show what leaders worry about and mandates carry legal consequences, but either can crowd out higher risks unless the CAE weighs them openly.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan): weigh each board, management, advisory or ad hoc request against risk, resources and benefit, and hold back hours for contingencies.
Must: tell the board and senior management in time about conflicting demands, such as a request to swap planned assurance for advisory work.
Must (Standard 9.1): understand how the organization identifies and manages its compliance with laws and regulations.
May: find mandates in board minutes, talks with the chief compliance officer and regulators' communications.
Should: consider engagements that law or regulation requires, and schedule around external audits and regulatory reviews.
KaiSip's reading: a low risk score does not remove a legal duty.
subtopics.example: A Kenyan insurer's audit committee chair asks for a claims fraud review, and the chief financial officer wants advice on an expense tool in place of the planned treasury audit. CAE Wanjiru scores both, uses reserved hours for the claims review, and reports the swap request to the board and senior management as a conflicting demand.

review: Trace each request received in the year to a documented decision
Compare the plan's mandated engagements with the regulatory requirements register
Inspect board minutes for reports of conflicting demands
evidence: Request log showing source, risk score and decision
Register of laws and regulations that require internal audit work
Board minutes approving significant changes to the plan
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive log every request with its risk score and report conflicting demands to the board promptly.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves significant plan changes (see 3B2.3)

subtopics.isaca_rule: A request is an input, not an order: weigh it against risk and resources, and report conflicting demands to the board and senior management (a must). Should: consider engagements that law or regulation requires.

exam_traps.trap: A request from an audit committee member goes straight into the plan.
exam_traps.why: It is weighed against risk and planned work. If it displaces significant work, the change needs the board's approval (see 3B2.3).

exam_traps.trap: A legally required engagement can be dropped when its risk score is low.
exam_traps.why: KaiSip's reading: the duty comes from the law, not the ranking. The considerations name legally required engagements among the things the CAE should consider, without ranking them.

key_terms.definition: Competing requests for internal audit services from major stakeholders, such as swapping planned assurance for advice.
Money or hours held back for needed plan changes nobody could foresee.

subtopics.name: Trends, Organizational Change and Emerging Technologies
subtopics.definition: Emerging risks are new or fast-changing exposures, from market shifts, organizational change or new technology, that the chief audit executive (CAE) tracks for the plan.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A plan built on last year's risks misses what is coming, such as AI, blockchain or robotic process automation. Early spotting lets the CAE offer foresight, not hindsight.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan): run a routine for spotting and rating new and emerging risks that are significant enough to plan for.
May (Standard 11.1): gather views from the board and senior management, industry news, regulatory changes, surveys, interviews and workshops.
Must (Standard 9.4): update the plan in time when the organization changes, such as through a merger, restructuring, new market or new system.
Knowledge (NIST AI RMF 3.6): de-identifying data supports privacy, yet AI adds privacy risk: it can infer who people are or private facts about them.
Sound practice (The IIA's AI Auditing Framework): the organization's risk assessment should cover AI; internal audit can inventory AI use in its yearly work.
Knowledge (NIST SP 800-213, IR 8259 Rev. 1): connected devices become system elements; many lack laptops' security functions, like updates or changeable passwords, so adding them can change risk.
subtopics.example: A Norwegian logistics firm tracks pallets with internet-connected sensors and lets warehouse staff use a generative AI tool. CAE Ingrid adds both to the risk assessment and reranks the units; a data-protection review now outranks a low-risk travel audit, so Ingrid proposes the swap to the board.

review: Inspect the risk assessment for new and emerging risks and their sources
Compare recent organizational changes with updates made to the plan
Trace each emerging risk to a documented planning decision
evidence: Risk assessment versions showing when each new risk was added
Notes of horizon-scanning meetings with senior management
Training records on emerging technologies for internal audit staff
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive record each emerging risk's source, rating and planning decision in the risk assessment.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves significant plan changes (see 3B2.3)

subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan for risks forming now. Should: keep a process for new and emerging risks. A new technology is a risk to rank, not an automatic engagement.

exam_traps.trap: Emerging technology risks can wait until an incident happens.
exam_traps.why: The plan should consider significant emerging risks; waiting for an incident gives hindsight, not foresight.

exam_traps.trap: Every new technology the organization adopts needs its own engagement this year.
exam_traps.why: It is ranked in the risk assessment like any other risk and planned when its risk warrants it.

key_terms.definition: A new or fast-changing risk with little history, whose likelihood and impact are still uncertain.
Common usage: systematically watching trends and developments for the risks and opportunities ahead.
Knowledge (NIST IR 8202): a blockchain guards published entries, but nothing within it confirms that what a person or sensor entered matches the real event.
Knowledge (NIST IR 8202): a blockchain only authorized members may publish to; its published entries resist and show tampering, though not strictly immutable.

subtopics.name: Topical Requirements and Audit Cycles in the Plan
subtopics.definition: At plan level, a Topical Requirement governs how a topic in scope is covered; an audit cycle sets how often an area is revisited.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Two common errors: thinking a Topical Requirement forces its topic into every plan, or that a cycle replaces risk ranking.
how_it_works: Must: a Topical Requirement applies when its topic is a planned engagement's subject, arises during an engagement, or is requested outside the plan.
May (user guides): once risk puts the topic in the plan, spread its requirements across one or more engagements, recorded in the plan or the workpapers.
Must: keep evidence that each requirement was assessed for applicability, with any exclusion's reason; quality assessments evaluate conformance.
Sound practice: check The IIA's CIA exam pages for which Topical Requirements are testable on your exam date; Cybersecurity already is.
Common usage: an audit cycle is a set revisit interval, driven by a law or regulator, the time since the last engagement, or limited resources.
KaiSip's reading (Standard 9.4): a cycle never replaces the annual risk assessment, and higher risk brings an area forward.
subtopics.example: At a Singapore hospital group, the risk assessment ranks cybersecurity high. CAE Wei Ling plans two engagements this year, one on cyber governance and risk management and one on controls, records which requirements each covers, and keeps the yearly pharmacy audit the health regulator requires.

review: Inspect the applicability record for each Topical Requirement in planned engagements
Trace each excluded requirement to a documented reason
Compare cycle-driven engagements with the current risk ranking
evidence: Topical Requirement applicability matrix with reasons for exclusions
Plan mapping each requirement to the engagements that cover it
Law, regulation or board decision setting a required frequency
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive map each applicable Topical Requirement to planned engagements and record every exclusion's reason.
audit_focus.decides: The quality team and external assessors judge Topical Requirement conformance

subtopics.isaca_rule: A Topical Requirement applies when its topic is planned, arises in an engagement or is requested, and sets the floor for assurance. A cycle says when to look again, never how big the risk is.

exam_traps.trap: A Topical Requirement makes its topic a mandatory engagement every year.
exam_traps.why: Risk assessment decides what is planned; the requirement governs the work once its topic is in scope.

exam_traps.trap: An area on a three-year cycle need not be reassessed between visits.
exam_traps.why: The risk assessment runs at least annually, whatever the cycle says.

key_terms.definition: The documented check of each requirement in a Topical Requirement: it applies here, or it is excluded for a stated reason.
Common usage: a set interval for revisiting an area, fixed by law, a regulator or the plan's own rotation.
The IIA's companion to a Topical Requirement explaining how to apply it; it joins the exam reference list when The IIA adds its requirement.

subtopics.memory_aid: Planned, found or requested: the Topical Requirement applies.

topics.overview: The plan turns the chief audit executive's documented risk assessment into engagements the board approves. This topic covers how risks are assessed and ranked, how the plan stays tied to strategy and stakeholders, and what forces a timely update.
can_do: Describe the organizationwide risk assessment and how it ranks auditable units
Describe how the plan stays aligned with both strategies and with what the board and senior management expect
Recognize events that call for a prompt plan update and how urgent changes reach the board

subtopics.name: The Organizationwide Risk Assessment and Ranking
subtopics.definition: The organizationwide risk assessment is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) documented, at least annual review of strategies, objectives and risks that decides which engagements the plan proposes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a documented, current assessment the plan reflects habit or the loudest voice, and the board cannot see why some high risks go unaudited.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan): document the assessment at least annually, with board and senior management input and the CAE's understanding of governance, risk management and control processes.
Should: rank units by their level of risk against the known effectiveness of their controls, and count opportunities as well as threats.
Common usage: impact and likelihood scales; the Standards set no scale.
Must (Standard 9.3 Methodologies): the CAE sets a documented method for developing the plan.
Must: the plan weighs coverage of IT governance, fraud risk, how well the compliance and ethics programs work, and other high-risk areas, and names its resources.
Should: show each engagement's rationale, the assurance and advisory mix, reserved hours, and the engagements that more resources would allow.
subtopics.example: At a Brazilian consumer bank, CAE Rafael scores 60 auditable units on impact and likelihood, lowering scores where recent tests showed controls working. Mobile lending ranks first, branch petty cash last. The draft plan states each engagement's rationale and names five more engagements that two extra auditors would allow.

review: Inspect the risk assessment's date, inputs and scoring method
Trace the top-ranked units to scheduled engagements
Compare high-risk areas without assurance with the rationale reported
evidence: Scoring worksheet with risk and control ratings for each unit
Documented risk assessment dated within the last year
Notes of planning interviews with board members and senior managers
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive document the scoring method and show the board the rationale for each proposed engagement.
audit_focus.decides: Plan approval sits with the board (see 3B2.2)

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rank by risk after controls, in writing, at least annually, with board and senior management input. The Standards fix no formula; they fix the documented assessment and the coverage the plan must consider.

exam_traps.trap: Roll last year's plan forward; risks rarely change in a year.
exam_traps.why: The plan must rest on a documented risk assessment done at least annually. A rotation can inform timing, never replace the assessment.

exam_traps.trap: The Standards require a five-point impact and likelihood scale.
exam_traps.why: No scale is prescribed. What is required is a documented, risk-based assessment informed by the board and senior management.

key_terms.definition: The list of engagements internal audit intends to carry out in a period, chosen by risk.
The stated reason an engagement is proposed, such as its risk level, a theme, a legal requirement or the time since the last one.

subtopics.name: Keeping the Plan Aligned With Strategy and Stakeholders
subtopics.definition: Plan alignment means the internal audit plan supports the organization's objectives, delivers the function's own strategy, and reflects what the board and senior management expect.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A plan that ignores strategy audits yesterday's priorities; one built without stakeholders' views loses their support and the board's approval.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan): the plan supports the organization's objectives and considers the mandate and the full range of agreed services.
Essential condition (for the board or senior management, not a requirement on internal audit): the board and senior management share their views on strategies, objectives and risks.
KaiSip's reading: the internal audit strategy (topic 3A3) sets direction; the plan delivers it, including the assurance and advisory balance.
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) discusses the plan with the board and senior management, and only the board gives approval (see Who decides).
Must: tell both bodies, in time, the impact of resource limits on coverage and why any high-risk area has no assurance engagement.
Must (Standard 6.3): coordinate the function's board communications with senior management.
subtopics.example: A Canadian university's board moves much of its teaching online. CAE Amara moves an online-exam integrity review ahead of a parking audit and shows which strategic objective each engagement serves. Amara discusses the draft with senior management, then takes it to the audit committee for approval.

review: Trace each planned engagement to an organizational objective or key risk
Inspect minutes for discussion with senior management and board approval
Inspect the strategy's targets against the plan's mix of services
evidence: Signed minute of the meeting where the plan was adopted
Notes of planning meetings with senior management
Plan showing each engagement's link to an objective
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive show the board how each engagement supports an objective and where coverage falls short.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the internal audit plan and significant changes to it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Senior management informs the plan; the board approves it. The CAE ties the plan to objectives and strategy and tells both bodies in time what it cannot cover, and why.

exam_traps.trap: The plan needs approval from both senior management and the board.
exam_traps.why: Discussion is with both; approval is the board's alone. Joint approval was the older rule.

exam_traps.trap: A high-risk area may be dropped quietly when resources are short.
exam_traps.why: Must: the CAE tells the board and senior management in time the impact of resource limits and why the area has no assurance engagement.

key_terms.definition: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
Keeping the plan tied to the organization's objectives, the function's strategy and what the board and senior management expect.
Board and senior management activities, not requirements on them, that Domain III lists as necessary for an effective internal audit function.

subtopics.memory_aid: Senior management informs; the board approves.

subtopics.name: A Dynamic Plan and the Events That Change It
subtopics.definition: A dynamic plan is revised in time as the business, its risks or its controls change, with each significant change approved by the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Risks do not wait for next year. A plan that cannot move leaves new risks uncovered; one that moves without approval weakens the board's oversight.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan): update the plan in time for changes in business, risks, operations, programs, systems, controls and culture.
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) tells the board and senior management in time about resource limits, uncovered high-risk areas, conflicting demands, and scope or access limits.
Must: discuss significant interim changes with the board and senior management; the board approves them.
Should: agree with the board and senior management what counts as a significant change, and record the criteria in the methodologies.
May: in a fast-changing environment, update the plan every six months, quarterly or even monthly.

rows.label: A change outside the agreed significance criteria
cells: Adjusts the schedule; KaiSip's reading: report it in the next regular update
Not a significant change, so no separate board approval

rows.label: Work on a significant risk canceled or postponed
cells: Discusses it with the board and senior management

rows.label: An urgent new risk before the next board meeting
cells: The board, formally, as soon as possible

rows.label: Resources cut during the year
cells: Reports the impact on coverage in time (a must)
Significant changes that follow go to the board

subtopics.example: Two months into the year, a Thai food exporter's largest customer demands new traceability data. CAE Somchai proposes bringing a supplier traceability review forward in place of a lower-risk fleet audit, tells the chief executive and the audit committee chair the same day, and seeks the committee's formal approval at a special meeting.

review: Compare plan versions with the dates of major organizational events
Trace each significant change to board approval or immediate notice
Inspect the agreed criteria that define a significant change
evidence: Version history of the plan with the reason for each change
Board minutes or notices approving significant interim changes
Methodology section setting the significant-change protocol
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive keep a dated log of plan changes showing which reached the board and when.
audit_focus.decides: Sign-off for a major revision belongs to the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: The plan is a living document: update it in time, discuss significant changes with the board and senior management, and get the board's approval. If urgent, tell the board at once and approve formally soon after (a should).

exam_traps.trap: Once approved, the plan is fixed until next year.
exam_traps.why: Must: the plan is dynamic and updated in time; significant changes are discussed with both bodies and approved by the board.

exam_traps.trap: An urgent change can be made now and reported to the board at year end.
exam_traps.why: Should: inform the board immediately and get formal approval as soon as possible.

key_terms.definition: A plan change meeting criteria agreed by the CAE, the board and senior management, such as canceling or postponing work on a significant risk.
A plan revised in time as the organization and its risks change, rather than fixed for the year.

subtopics.memory_aid: Significant change: discuss with both bodies, board approves; if urgent, tell the board now.

topics.overview: Internal audit is not the only source of assurance. This topic names the other providers, the ways the chief audit executive coordinates coverage with them, and the tests applied before relying on their work, which never moves responsibility for internal audit's conclusions.
can_do: Name the other providers of assurance inside and outside the organization, and how the CAE finds them
Identify ways to coordinate coverage, including an assurance map and combined assurance
Identify the tests for relying on another provider and what reliance never transfers

subtopics.name: Who the Other Assurance Providers Are
subtopics.definition: Other assurance providers are the internal functions and outside parties, besides internal audit, whose work gives the board or management confidence about risks and controls.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Ignoring them means paying twice for the same checks and still missing gaps. Knowing who covers what comes before coordinating it.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.5 Coordination and Reliance): the chief audit executive (CAE) coordinates with internal and external assurance providers and considers relying on their work.
KaiSip's reading (Standard 9.5): internal providers include compliance, risk management, information security, health and safety, legal, environmental, financial control and quality assurance.
KaiSip's reading (Three Lines Model statement, 2026): external providers include the external auditor, regulators and accreditation bodies.
Should: find them by talking with senior management and reviewing the reporting structure and board agendas and minutes.
Must: coordinate so that duplicated work falls and gaps in key risk coverage show (Standard 9.5's stated aims).
Should: evaluate second-line work before relying on it, because the second line is part of management (see 3B3.3).
subtopics.example: New CAE Sipho at a South African mining group reads two years of board minutes and the organization chart. Sipho lists the safety inspectorate, environmental compliance, IT security, the external auditor and the mines regulator as assurance providers, and meets each to learn what they cover and when.

review: Compare the provider inventory with the organization chart and board minutes
Inspect records of coordination meetings with each provider
evidence: Inventory of assurance providers with scope and reporting line
Notes of meetings agreeing roles with each provider
Board minutes discussing assurance coverage across providers
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive keep a current inventory of assurance providers, their scope and their reporting lines.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides on reliance and stays responsible for conclusions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Map every source of assurance before planning coverage. Must: coordinate with internal and external providers and consider relying on them. Second-line work is evaluated before internal audit leans on it.

exam_traps.trap: Only internal audit is an assurance provider; compliance just informs management.
exam_traps.why: The Standards name compliance, risk management and similar functions as internal providers of assurance, and the CAE must coordinate with them.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit must never rely on second-line work because the second line is not independent.
exam_traps.why: Reliance is possible after evaluating objectivity, competency and care; the reporting line affects how much weight the work gets.

key_terms.definition: Any internal or external party that gives assurance, such as compliance, risk management or the external auditor.
Management's specialist roles, such as risk management and compliance, that support, monitor and challenge the first line and give targeted assurance.
The IIA's model of who owns risk, who supports and challenges, and who gives independent assurance.

subtopics.name: Coordinating Coverage: Assurance Maps and Combined Assurance
subtopics.definition: Coordinating coverage means aligning what each assurance provider examines, when and how, so key risks are covered once and well, with gaps and overlaps visible.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Uncoordinated reviews tire the business with repeat visits yet leave risks nobody tests. The board needs one coherent view of assurance.
how_it_works: May (examples in Standard 9.5): align the nature, extent and timing of work, agree common terms, share work programs and reports, and combine results.
May: build an assurance map that sets significant risks against their providers and rates the assurance each gives, exposing gaps and duplication.
May: use combined assurance to cut repeat reviews; The IIA's 2026 statement calls a more structured, mature form of coordination and reliance integrated assurance.
Sound practice: keep coordination informal in small organizations and formal in large or regulated ones, and weigh confidentiality rules before sharing.
Must: when coordination fails, the chief audit executive (CAE) raises the concern with senior management first, then with the board where needed.
subtopics.example: At a German auto parts maker, CAE Lukas maps 14 risk categories against internal audit, quality assurance, information security, compliance and the external auditor. Three providers test supplier quality; nobody tests cyber recovery. Lukas agrees with quality assurance to stop duplicating supplier tests and shows the board the cyber gap.

review: Inspect risk categories the map rates as uncovered or covered twice
Compare the map's ratings with the providers' actual reports
Trace stalled coordination to concerns raised with senior management
evidence: Current assurance map with a coverage rating for each risk
Joint schedule of engagements signed off by each provider
Correspondence raising coordination concerns with senior management
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive maintain an assurance map and present its gaps and overlaps to the board.
audit_focus.decides: Escalation order when providers will not cooperate: senior management, then the board if necessary

subtopics.isaca_rule: Coordinate to remove both gaps and duplication. An assurance map is a useful tool, not a requirement. Must: when coordination fails, raise it with senior management first and the board if necessary.

exam_traps.trap: When a provider will not coordinate, the CAE goes straight to the board.
exam_traps.why: Must: the concern goes to senior management and, if necessary, the board; going to the board first skips a step.

exam_traps.trap: An assurance map is a mandatory part of every internal audit plan.
exam_traps.why: It is one coordination method in the considerations. What is required is coordination itself and considering reliance.

key_terms.definition: A table of significant risks and who gives assurance over each.
Coordinating internal audit's assurance work with other providers' so key risks are covered without repeated reviews.
The common name, used in The IIA's 2026 statement, for a structured, mature form of coordination and reliance across the lines; not required.

subtopics.memory_aid: Map the coverage, share the work, escalate to senior management first.

subtopics.name: Deciding Whether to Rely on Another Provider
subtopics.definition: Deciding on reliance means the chief audit executive (CAE) tests whether another provider's work is trustworthy enough to use instead of internal audit's own testing.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Good reliance extends coverage into specialist areas and saves testing. Blind reliance imports someone else's errors into internal audit's conclusions, which remain the CAE's responsibility.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 9.5 Coordination and Reliance): use a set method to evaluate the provider's independence, objectivity, competency and due care, and understand its objectives, scope and results.
Should: check conflicts of interest and disclosures, reporting lines, experience and certifications, care in planning and review, and whether findings rest on sound evidence.
Must: document the basis for reliance; the CAE stays responsible for internal audit's conclusions.
May: if the work fails the test, internal auditors retest it and gather more information, or perform the assurance themselves.
Should: document long-term reliance agreements and reevaluate reliance periodically.
Must (Standard 11.3): disclose reliance in a business-unit or organization-level conclusion.
subtopics.example: A Spanish airline's safety department tests pilot training records every quarter. Before relying on it, CAE Lucia confirms the testers are licensed, do not report to flight operations and keep evidence for each result. Lucia reperforms a small sample, documents the basis, and discloses the reliance in the year-end safety conclusion.

review: Reperform a sample of the provider's tests before relying on them
Inspect the documented basis for each reliance decision
Compare reliance disclosed in wider conclusions with reliance actually taken
evidence: Reperformance results for a sample of the provider's work
Reliance memo covering independence, competence, method and evidence
Signed agreement on scope and evidence for long-term reliance
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive keep a reliance memo per provider and refresh it when its scope or staff change.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides on reliance and answers for the conclusions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rely after evaluating, never on reputation. Must: document the basis; the CAE stays responsible for internal audit's conclusions and discloses reliance in any wider conclusion. Work that fails the test is retested or redone.

exam_traps.trap: Relying on a well-known consulting firm's report moves responsibility for that conclusion to the firm.
exam_traps.why: Must: the CAE stays responsible for the conclusions the internal audit function reaches, whoever did the underlying work.

exam_traps.trap: A provider with a strong reputation can be relied on without review.
exam_traps.why: Should: evaluate conflicts of interest, reporting lines, qualifications, method and evidence first. Must: document the basis for the reliance.

key_terms.definition: Using another party's work or information instead of repeating it, after judging it trustworthy.
The documented reasons the CAE judged another provider's work trustworthy enough to use.

subtopics.memory_aid: Test it, document it, own it, disclose it.

key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
key_terminologies.Board: The highest governing body, such as the directors or audit committee; where several govern, the body (or bodies) empowered to give internal audit its mandate.
key_terminologies.Topical Requirement: A mandatory baseline for assurance engagements on a named subject, such as cybersecurity; recommended for advisory work.
key_terminologies.Auditable unit: A part of the organization that could be the subject of an engagement, such as a business unit, process, program or system.
key_terminologies.Organizationwide risk assessment: The CAE's documented review, at least yearly, of the organization's strategies, objectives and risks on which the plan is built.
key_terminologies.Audit universe: Internal audit's list of the units, processes and systems that could be audited.
key_terminologies.Cross-cutting risk: A risk that spans several units or processes, such as fraud or third-party risk, and needs a joined-up evaluation.
key_terminologies.Consideration for Implementation: A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
key_terminologies.Conflicting demands: Competing requests for internal audit services from major stakeholders, such as swapping planned assurance for advice.
key_terminologies.Contingency reserve: Money or hours held back for needed plan changes nobody could foresee.
key_terminologies.Emerging risk: A new or fast-changing risk with little history, whose likelihood and impact are still uncertain.
key_terminologies.Horizon scanning: Common usage: systematically watching trends and developments for the risks and opportunities ahead.
key_terminologies.Applicability assessment: The documented check of each requirement in a Topical Requirement: it applies here, or it is excluded for a stated reason.
key_terminologies.Audit cycle: Common usage: a set interval for revisiting an area, fixed by law, a regulator or the plan's own rotation.
key_terminologies.User guide: The IIA's companion to a Topical Requirement explaining how to apply it; it joins the exam reference list when The IIA adds its requirement.
key_terminologies.Internal audit plan: The list of engagements internal audit intends to carry out in a period, chosen by risk.
key_terminologies.Engagement rationale: The stated reason an engagement is proposed, such as its risk level, a theme, a legal requirement or the time since the last one.
key_terminologies.Senior management: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
key_terminologies.Plan alignment: Keeping the plan tied to the organization's objectives, the function's strategy and what the board and senior management expect.
key_terminologies.Essential conditions: Board and senior management activities, not requirements on them, that Domain III lists as necessary for an effective internal audit function.
key_terminologies.Significant change: A plan change meeting criteria agreed by the CAE, the board and senior management, such as canceling or postponing work on a significant risk.
key_terminologies.Dynamic plan: A plan revised in time as the organization and its risks change, rather than fixed for the year.
key_terminologies.Assurance provider: Any internal or external party that gives assurance, such as compliance, risk management or the external auditor.
key_terminologies.Second line: Management's specialist roles, such as risk management and compliance, that support, monitor and challenge the first line and give targeted assurance.
key_terminologies.Three Lines Model: The IIA's model of who owns risk, who supports and challenges, and who gives independent assurance.
key_terminologies.Assurance map: A table of significant risks and who gives assurance over each.
key_terminologies.Combined assurance: Coordinating internal audit's assurance work with other providers' so key risks are covered without repeated reviews.
key_terminologies.Integrated assurance: The common name, used in The IIA's 2026 statement, for a structured, mature form of coordination and reliance across the lines; not required.
key_terminologies.Reliance: Using another party's work or information instead of repeating it, after judging it trustworthy.
key_terminologies.Basis for reliance: The documented reasons the CAE judged another provider's work trustworthy enough to use.
